The people (like me and a number of other seismologists at Saint Louis University) who research these earthquakes have been busily working on figuring out a way to distinguish between the still viable hypotheses with the observations that are available.

*Very* much an area of active research.

The textbook standard solution ("dehydration embrittlement" related to volumetric change) is not something that works with modern understanding of the volumetric changes that happen with dehydration reactions (these don't reduce the confining pressure, and should *prohibit* earthquakes).

Earthquakes at these depths are generally located within parts of the slab (independently imaged by other techniques) should be mostly relatively cold, but the confining pressure at these depths should make the rock too strong to rupture with any reasonably valued tectonic forces.

I take issue with this bit:
"it is generally unsurprising when we see earthquakes at 100, 200, even up to 300 kilometers depth"

By what we know from rock mechanics, these events shouldn't happen. It requires a (still contested) mechanism to cause.
